results.name: n1_set_mean_variance
results.description: Variance across one-example sets of each set's mean yes rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalization differs more between lone examples than the model's single global doubt/flat-rate mixture allows (observed < null: model over-differentiates lone examples).
results.code:
# name: n1_set_mean_variance
# description: Variance across one-example sets of each set's mean yes rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalization differs more between lone examples than the model's single global doubt/flat-rate mixture allows (observed < null: model over-differentiates lone examples).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values[one]
    u, inv = np.unique(s.values[one], return_inverse=True)
    m = np.bincount(inv, weights=r) / np.bincount(inv)
    return float(np.var(m))

results.name: n1_parity_match_gap
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate on targets with the example's parity minus yes rate on opposite-parity targets; observed > null means the model's flat-rate doubt dilutes property-based (parity) generalization from a lone example too much (observed < null: model over-weights parity).
results.code:
# name: n1_parity_match_gap
# description: For one-example sets, yes rate on targets with the example's parity minus yes rate on opposite-parity targets; observed > null means the model's flat-rate doubt dilutes property-based (parity) generalization from a lone example too much (observed < null: model over-weights parity).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(one, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    same = one & (t % 2 == e % 2)
    diff = one & (t % 2 != e % 2)
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())

results.name: n1_distance_gradient
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed > null means the model still makes lone-example generalization too flat in magnitude, observed < null means the model's band is still steeper than people's (who are nearly flat in distance).
results.code:
# name: n1_distance_gradient
# description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed > null means the model still makes lone-example generalization too flat in magnitude, observed < null means the model's band is still steeper than people's (who are nearly flat in distance).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(one, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).values
    d = np.abs(df["target"].astype(int).values - e)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = one & (d <= 10)
    b = one & (d > 30)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: multi_item_mean_variance
results.description: Over multi-example (2-4) sets only, variance across (set, target) pairs of the pair's mean yes rate; observed > null means people separate endorsed from rejected targets more sharply than the model's overlap judgment (model too graded/under-confident on multi-example sets), observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: multi_item_mean_variance
# description: Over multi-example (2-4) sets only, variance across (set, target) pairs of the pair's mean yes rate; observed > null means people separate endorsed from rejected targets more sharply than the model's overlap judgment (model too graded/under-confident on multi-example sets), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    multi = (s.str.count(",") > 0).values
    key = (s.values[multi] + "|" + df["target"].astype(str).values[multi])
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values[multi]
    u, inv = np.unique(key, return_inverse=True)
    m = np.bincount(inv, weights=r) / np.bincount(inv)
    return float(np.var(m))

results.name: multi_small_target_gap
results.description: Over multi-example sets, yes rate on targets 1-10 minus yes rate on targets 11-100; observed < null means the model over-endorses small targets (which belong to many concepts such as squares, powers, small multiples) relative to people, observed > null means it under-endorses them.
results.code:
# name: multi_small_target_gap
# description: Over multi-example sets, yes rate on targets 1-10 minus yes rate on targets 11-100; observed < null means the model over-endorses small targets (which belong to many concepts such as squares, powers, small multiples) relative to people, observed > null means it under-endorses them.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    multi = (s.str.count(",") > 0).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = multi & (t <= 10)
    b = multi & (t > 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: multi_set_size_trend
results.description: Yes rate on 2-example sets minus yes rate on 4-example sets; observed > null means people narrow their generalization with more examples more than the model does (model under-produces the size-principle tightening), observed < null the reverse.

results.name: n1_multiple_relation_gap
results.description: For one-example sets and same-parity targets only, yes rate when target and example are multiples/divisors of each other (target != example, example > 1) minus yes rate otherwise; observed > null means people generalize along the multiplicative relation more than the model (which lacks a 'multiples of the example' concept beyond fixed moduli 3-12) predicts.
results.code:
# name: n1_multiple_relation_gap
# description: For one-example sets and same-parity targets only, yes rate when target and example are multiples/divisors of each other (target != example, example > 1) minus yes rate otherwise; observed > null means people generalize along the multiplicative relation more than the model (which lacks a 'multiples of the example' concept beyond fixed moduli 3-12) predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(one, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ok = one & (e > 1) & (t != e) & (t % 2 == e % 2)
    es = np.where(e > 0, e, 1)
    rel = ((t % es == 0) | (es % t == 0))
    a = ok & rel
    b = ok & ~rel
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: shared_digit_match_yes
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a final digit, yes rate on targets that also end in that digit (excluding targets that are themselves examples); observed > null means the model under-produces endorsement of a visible final-digit rule, observed < null over-produces it.
